summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is hostile to transgender visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with reporting indicating that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Yogyakarta is not among the two provinces where the Human Dignity Trust records provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity under regional religious law, so the provincial Sharia penalties recorded in Aceh and South Sumatra do not extend to this special region.

Within that national exposure, Yogyakarta presents a regulatory layer that is discriminatory on paper but unproven in operation against transgender people. OutRight Action International's 2022 study 'Creeping Criminalisation' maps national laws and regional regulations that violate the human rights of women and LGBTIQ people, examining regulations in eight focus provinces including Yogyakarta, and finds significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The dossier documents no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people in Yogyakarta itself, and OutRight states its findings are valid for regions beyond its focus set.

The clearest enforcement-adjacent event on record is the closure of the trans-Muslim religious school in this special region. On the night of 24 February 2016, Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, where trans women study Islam, was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal it; the district head justified the closure on the grounds that the school lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site, and the shutdown proceeded on administrative and community grounds with no provincial anti-trans statute cited. Governor Sultan Hamengku Buwono X publicly urged restraint on both sides, describing LGBT people as fellow children of the nation and saying the regional government would study the issue. BBC Indonesia's report describes rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta', and a witness to the closure meeting reported that a Front Jihad Islam leader vowed to keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather.

For a traveller the practical exposure in Yogyakarta is therefore the national criminalisation regime combined with an untested discriminatory regulatory layer and documented local hostility from hardline groups, rather than a provincial anti-trans law with a known enforcement record.
tangentialFactors:
Yogyakarta sits inside a national pattern that the sources describe as tightening. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

National enforcement practice is not limited to prosecution. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and Aceh's punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

OutRight's mapping shows that Yogyakarta's discriminatory regulations are not an isolated local artefact but part of a set shared with Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi and South Sumatra, with much overlap and significant regional variation in the restrictions imposed on transgender people.
localsOnly:
OutRight's 2022 study 'Creeping Criminalisation', by Katjasungkana and Wieringa, examines regional regulations in eight focus provinces and identifies discriminatory provisions affecting dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, while noting that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

Regional authorities in Yogyakarta act on permit compliance rather than on a trans-specific statute: the Banguntapan district head justified the February 2016 closure of the Al-Fatah waria pesantren on the grounds that it lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. The closure meeting on 24 February 2016 at the Jagalan ward office was attended by ward and residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in an earlier session on 19 February, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief.

The Al-Fatah pesantren was operating again years after the 2016 closure. DW Indonesia reported on 21 June 2021 that Yogyakarta's trans women, most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the pesantren, saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic, were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', and struggled to pay rent and buy food; the article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances.

Founder Shinta Ratri stated that about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. Governor Sultan Hamengku Buwono X's public response in 2016 was to urge restraint on both sides, call LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' and say the regional government would study the issue.

Unresolved: the specific text of Yogyakarta's regional regulations on dress codes, curfews or the public appearance of transgender people is not quoted in the sources reviewed here, so the presence of any such provision in this special region is asserted only at the level of OutRight's mapping of the eight-province set.

Unresolved: no source in this inventory documents an enacted anti-LGBT or anti-trans bylaw in the Special Region of Yogyakarta, nor any police action against a transgender visitor here; the 2016 pesantren closure proceeded on administrative and religious grounds with no provincial anti-trans statute cited.

Not sourced: whether the dispute over the Al-Fatah pesantren was resolved after the June 2021 reporting, and whether any permit application or reinstatement followed the February 2016 agreement to shut the school.

Not sourced: the current regional-government position on the October 2025 presidential decree listing LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy, and whether Yogyakarta has adopted any of the national anti-LGBTQ+ directives at regional level.
